claim: Lightning can strike the same place multiple times, with tall structures like the Empire State Building being hit about 20-25 times per year.
support: Empirical monitoring data from instrumented skyscrapers shows repeated lightning attachments to the same structure across seasons, consistent with the claim that the Empire State Building is struck many times per year.
Electrical breakdown physics favors the tallest conductive points as attachment sites, making repeat strikes to the same place not only possible but likely, supporting the claim’s general truth.

Lightning protection systems employ air terminals designed to intercept strikes repeatedly rather than prevent them, which aligns with reports of the Empire State Building receiving on the order of dozens of strikes per year.

Historical records and utility/meteorological reports document multi-decade patterns of frequent strikes to tall towers, corroborating the claim’s assertion of roughly 20–25 hits per year for structures like the Empire State Building.
attack: Year-to-year lightning activity varies substantially; in some years New York City’s storm frequency would yield counts below or above 20–25, so the stated range may not consistently hold true.

Different counting conventions (flashes vs. strokes vs. attachment points) can inflate or deflate reported ‘strike’ numbers, meaning the specific figure of 20–25 may not be accurate under all definitions.

Urban skyline changes and modifications to lightning protection systems can redistribute attachment points among nearby tall structures, potentially lowering the Empire State Building’s recent strike frequency compared with the cited range.

claim: The human heart beats approximately 100,000 times per day and pumps about 2,000 gallons of blood through the body's circulatory system.
support: Using a typical adult resting heart rate of about 70 beats per minute yields roughly 70 × 60 × 24 ≈ 100,800 beats per day, which supports the claim’s ~100,000 beats figure as approximately true.

A standard resting cardiac output of about 5 liters per minute totals ~7,200 liters per day, which is about 1,900 U.S. gallons—close enough to substantiate the claim’s ~2,000 gallons as an approximate statement.

The claim’s use of “gallons” is ambiguous between U.S. (3.785 L) and Imperial (4.546 L) units; if interpreted as Imperial gallons, 2,000 gallons would imply ~9,092 liters per day, which conflicts with standard physiology, challenging the claim’s truthfulness as written.

The claim conjoins two approximations as if both are simultaneously true for a typical day and person; given individual variability, a heart rate that yields ~100,000 beats/day does not necessarily coincide with a daily pumped volume near 2,000 gallons, weakening the truth of the combined statement.

FDG-PET studies consistently localize about 20% of the body’s resting glucose utilization to the brain, corroborating the claim’s proportional energy use.

claim: Mount Everest grows approximately 4 millimeters taller each year due to the ongoing collision of the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates.

The ongoing convergence of the Indian and Eurasian plates (several cm/yr of shortening) drives crustal thickening and surface uplift in the High Himalaya, a mechanism that directly supports the claim’s approximate annual growth rate.

Geodynamic models of Himalayan orogenesis predict millimeter‑per‑year vertical velocities concentrated near the range crest, aligning with an average uplift of about 4 mm/yr at Everest over multi‑year timescales.
attack: No permanent GPS station sits on the summit itself; extrapolating a precise 4 mm/yr rate to the peak from nearby stations introduces uncertainty, so the specific quantitative claim may not be strictly true for Everest’s exact summit.

“Height” depends on the chosen reference (ellipsoid vs. geoid) and whether snow/ice depth is included; annual variations in these can exceed millimeters, making the unqualified statement about a 4 mm/yr increase potentially false in common measurement frameworks.

Erosion, rockfall, and freeze–thaw weathering at the summit can remove material at rates that partially offset tectonic uplift, so the net change in Everest’s elevation relative to sea level may be less than ~4 mm/yr or even negligible over certain intervals.

claim: The Eiffel Tower can be up to 6 inches taller during the summer than in winter because the iron structure expands when heated by the sun.

Empirical reports from the Eiffel Tower’s operators and engineering references state seasonal height changes around 15 cm, attributing the variation to thermal expansion of the iron structure.

The riveted, trussed geometry allows some thermal strain to be absorbed via joint clearances and lateral deformation; not all linear expansion converts into added vertical height, so the maximum net height increase may fall short of 6 inches even when members expand significantly.

Authoritative time zone standards (e.g., IANA TZ database) and annual global coverage list Kiritimati (Kiribati) as the first populated place to celebrate the New Year, which corroborates that Kiribati experiences the new year before any other country.

The current configuration of the Date Line places Kiribati’s eastern atolls on the ‘new day’ side, so as the Earth rotates, their local date advances ahead of all other nations, directly yielding an earlier New Year for Kiribati than anywhere else.

claim: A standard deck of playing cards has 52 factorial possible arrangements, which is approximately 8 followed by 67 zeros, meaning that every time you shuffle a deck thoroughly, you are almost certainly creating an arrangement that has never existed before in history.
support: Magnitude comparison: 52! ≈ 8.07×10^67 possible orders dwarfs any plausible count of all shuffles in human history (bounded by population × years × shuffles per second), so the chance a fresh, well-randomized shuffle matches any historical order is vanishingly small—hence it is almost certainly novel.

Birthday-paradox threshold: Repeats become likely only when the number of independent, near-uniform shuffles approaches √(52!) ≈ 10^34; humanity’s total shuffles are orders of magnitude below this, so the probability that your new shuffle duplicates any past order is effectively zero, supporting the claim’s “almost certainly.”
attack: Real-world shuffles are not perfectly uniform: human riffles and many common procedures overweight a tiny fraction of the 52! permutations and produce correlations, raising repeat probabilities above the uniform model the claim implicitly relies on; thus “almost certainly” can be overstated.

Apparent thoroughness can be deceptive: structured methods like near-perfect faro shuffles cycle through small subsets of permutations and can revisit previous orders in relatively few steps, so a deck shuffled this way is not “almost certainly” in a never-before-seen arrangement.

Ambiguity of what counts as the “same arrangement”: if arrangements are distinguished by the physical identity of cards (not just rank/suit order), then cross-history comparisons are ill-defined and the 52! argument no longer supports the claim; if only abstract ranks/suits matter, the claim may hold, but its truth hinges on this definition.

claim: The first successful vaccine was developed by Edward Jenner in 1796 to prevent smallpox, using material from cowpox lesions to provide immunity.

Jenner’s 1798 publication documented multiple successful cases following the 1796 procedure and spurred rapid replication by other physicians, reinforcing that his cowpox-based method reliably conferred smallpox immunity.

Historical and institutional consensus (e.g., major medical histories, public health authorities) explicitly identifies Jenner’s 1796 cowpox inoculation as the first successful “vaccine,” with the term itself derived from vacca (cow), aligning with the claim.

The swift replacement of riskier variolation by Jennerian vaccination and the rollout of organized vaccination programs soon after 1796 indicate real-world efficacy and novelty consistent with the claim.

Genetic and historical analyses suggest early vaccine strains were closer to vaccinia/horsepox rather than true cowpox, casting doubt on the claim’s specificity that cowpox lesion material was the source.

If “vaccine” is interpreted broadly to include earlier smallpox variolation (deliberate inoculation with smallpox), then preventive immunization predates 1796, undermining the “first” aspect of the claim.

Their observed behavior is almost exclusively short, explosive flights to escape danger or reach roosts, not continuous flight, which supports a very short recorded maximum like 13 seconds.
Domestication has selected for heavier bodies and productivity over flight, reducing endurance relative to wild ancestors and aligning with a brief longest recorded flight.

claim: The first email was sent in 1971 by computer engineer Ray Tomlinson, who also chose the @ symbol to separate the user name from the computer name in email addresses.

Authoritative institutions (e.g., Internet Society/Internet Hall of Fame, Smithsonian) attribute both the first network email and the choice of @ to Tomlinson in 1971, reflecting a strong historical consensus.

claim: The Nobel Prize cannot be awarded posthumously except in cases where the recipient dies after the announcement but before the December ceremony, a rule that has been in effect since 1974.

claim: The modern piano has 88 keys as a standard, with 52 white keys and 36 black keys, a configuration that was established by the 1880s to accommodate the range of most classical compositions.
support: The specific count of 88 keys split into 52 white and 36 black is the de facto specification of contemporary acoustic concert pianos, corroborated by manufacturer catalogs and reference materials, indicating the claim’s factual accuracy about modern standard configuration.

Historical records show Steinway popularized the 88‑key layout around 1880, and major makers followed in that decade, supporting the truth of the claim that the configuration was established by the 1880s.

By the late 19th century, composers had stretched keyboard ranges to the extremes approached by A0–C8, so settling on 88 keys matched the practical needs of the prevailing classical repertoire, lending credibility to the claim’s rationale about accommodating most compositions.

Conservatory curricula and notation conventions normalized around the 88‑key span by the end of the 19th century, consistent with the claim that an 88‑key standard had been established to serve the typical range expected in classical performance and study.

Calling 88 keys the standard for the ‘modern piano’ is imprecise because many modern instruments (e.g., 73‑ or 76‑key stage and digital pianos, and extended‑range 97‑key acoustics) deviate from 88, challenging the universality implied by the claim.

Documented expansions from 61 to 85 to 88 keys unfolded gradually over decades in the 19th century, indicating that the endpoint was an evolutionary compromise rather than a change explicitly targeted to fit the range of most compositions, which undercuts the claimed causal rationale.

claim: The Amazon River discharges more water into the ocean than the next seven largest rivers combined, accounting for approximately 20% of all fresh water that flows into the world's oceans.
support: Long-term gauge records at Óbidos and other stations consistently show an average Amazon discharge near 200,000–220,000 m³/s, while published sums of the next seven largest rivers fall below that total, directly supporting the claim’s comparative statement.

The Amazon’s drainage basin is the world’s largest and coincides with exceptionally high equatorial rainfall; these fundamentals yield a sustained outflow proportion that plausibly reaches roughly one-fifth of global riverine discharge, buttressing the 20% figure.

Independent satellite-based methods (e.g., GRACE gravimetry and altimetry-derived river heights) broadly corroborate in situ estimates of Amazon discharge and its dominance in the global river budget, reinforcing the claim’s magnitude.

The observed scale of the Amazon’s low-salinity surface plume in the Atlantic and its documented influence on regional salinity and carbon fluxes align with an outflow share on the order of 20%, lending empirical oceanographic support to the claim.

The truth of the comparison hinges on how rivers are defined and aggregated (e.g., treating the Ganges–Brahmaputra–Meghna as one system, inclusion of estuarine branches); different, defensible conventions can change the ranking and totals enough to challenge the claim.

If ‘all fresh water that flows into the world’s oceans’ is interpreted to include submarine groundwater discharge and ice melt, the Amazon’s share drops relative to the enlarged denominator, undermining the accuracy of the 20% figure.

Significant measurement uncertainties and data sparsity for some large tropical rivers (notably the Congo) mean their true averages could be higher than commonly cited, weakening confidence in the assertion that the Amazon exceeds the next seven combined.

claim: The average cloud weighs approximately 1.1 million pounds, as calculated from the typical density of water droplets suspended in the air and the volume of a cumulus cloud.
support: Using standard meteorological estimates for fair‑weather cumulus, a liquid water content around 0.5 g/m³ and a volume near 1 km³ give a water mass of ~5×10^5 kg, which converts to roughly 1.1 million pounds—matching the claimed figure.

Remote sensing retrievals (radar/lidar) commonly find liquid water paths of ~50–200 g/m² for small cumuli; with cloud depths of ~0.5–1 km this implies mean liquid water contents of ~0.1–0.4 g/m³ and kilometer‑scale horizontal extents, yielding a total water mass on the order of 10^6 pounds.

A mass of ~5×10^5 kg spread over a ~1 km² footprint would correspond to only a few millimeters of rain if condensed out, consistent with the non‑precipitating nature of typical fair‑weather cumulus and supporting the plausibility of the claimed weight.
attack: “Average cloud” is not well‑defined: clouds range from thin cirrus with negligible liquid to vast stratocumulus decks and deep convective towers, so a single average near 1.1 million pounds is unlikely to be true across the highly skewed population.

The calculation often assumes a ~1 km × 1 km × 1 km cumulus, but many common cumulus humilis are only a few hundred meters across and deep, reducing volume—and thus weight—by an order of magnitude below 1.1 million pounds.

Liquid water content in cumulus varies widely (roughly ~0.05–3 g/m³); using lower, yet typical, values for fair‑weather clouds yields masses far below 1.1 million pounds, so the specific numeric claim overstates its general truth.

claim: The first postage stamp, called the Penny Black, was issued in the United Kingdom in 1840 and featured a profile of Queen Victoria, revolutionizing mail delivery by requiring prepayment by the sender rather than payment by the recipient.

Rowland Hill’s reforms implemented with the Penny Black operationalized the prepayment model at scale, shifting postage costs to senders and establishing a durable norm of sender-paid mail.

claim: The caffeine in coffee reaches peak concentration in the bloodstream approximately 30 to 60 minutes after consumption, with a half-life of about 5 hours in the average adult, meaning it takes that long for the body to eliminate half of the consumed caffeine.
support: Controlled pharmacokinetic studies measuring plasma caffeine after coffee ingestion consistently report a Tmax in the 30–60 minute window, supporting the claim’s peak timing.

Caffeine elimination in healthy, non-smoking adults follows first-order kinetics with a central tendency around a 5-hour half-life, matching the claim’s statement about how long it takes to remove half the dose.
Risk assessments and clinical guidance commonly model caffeine with an approximate 5-hour half-life, indicating consensus that this is a reasonable average for adult metabolism.
Behavioral effects (alertness and sleep latency changes) persist for several hours in line with measured plasma levels, indirectly corroborating an elimination half-life near five hours.
attack: Interindividual variability (e.g., CYP1A2 genotype, liver function, smoking status) produces half-lives ranging roughly from 1.5 to over 10 hours, so a single “about 5 hours” figure can be inaccurate for many adults and overstates the claim’s generality.

Co-ingestion with food—especially high-fat meals—can delay gastrointestinal absorption, pushing the plasma peak beyond 60 minutes, which challenges the claim’s peak timing for typical breakfast coffee.

Caffeine can show secondary plasma peaks due to redistribution or enterohepatic recirculation, meaning a single, well-defined peak at 30–60 minutes is not universal, weakening the claimed timing as a general truth.

claim: The platypus is one of only five species of monotremes, or egg-laying mammals, and males possess venomous spurs on their hind legs that can deliver a painful sting capable of incapacitating small animals and causing severe pain in humans.

Clinical and case-report evidence shows platypus envenomation causes intense, prolonged pain and swelling in humans, and has been reported to incapacitate small animals such as dogs, supporting the claim’s description of effects.

The assertion that the sting can incapacitate small animals relies largely on anecdotal or uncontrolled reports; rigorous experimental evidence for reliable incapacitation across small species is limited.

claim: The first commercial barcode was scanned on a pack of Wrigley's Juicy Fruit chewing gum at a supermarket in Troy, Ohio on June 26, 1974, marking the beginning of widespread automated checkout systems in retail stores.

attack: The phrase “first commercial barcode” is too broad; barcodes were commercially scanned earlier in non‑retail contexts (e.g., KarTrak railroad identification in the late 1960s), so without specifying “retail UPC,” the claim is not strictly true.

Earlier retail barcode trials (e.g., RCA’s bull’s‑eye code tests with Kroger in the early 1970s) predate the Troy scan, weakening the claim that this specific event uniquely initiated retail automation.

claim: The first subway system in the world opened in London in 1863 and used steam-powered trains that ran through underground tunnels, initially carrying approximately 38,000 passengers on its opening day despite concerns about the safety and health effects of traveling beneath the earth.

Engineering documentation shows that the line used steam locomotives with condensers specifically adapted for underground operation, confirming that steam-powered trains ran through tunnels at launch.
Ticketing and ridership tallies from the opening day cite a figure in the high tens of thousands, with multiple sources reporting roughly 38,000 passengers, supporting the approximate number given.

Newspaper editorials, medical commentary, and parliamentary discussions from the period record explicit fears about air quality, ventilation, and structural risks underground, supporting the claim that it opened despite safety and health concerns.
attack: Some reputable sources report opening-day ridership as “over 30,000” rather than approximately 38,000, casting doubt on the numeric accuracy of the specific passenger figure stated.

claim: The first traffic light was installed in London in 1868 and was operated manually by a police officer, using red and green gas lamps to control horse-drawn carriage traffic, but it exploded less than a month after installation, injuring the operator.
support: Contemporary newspaper accounts (e.g., The Times in early January 1869) report a gas-signal explosion outside Parliament that injured the on-site constable, corroborating both the explosion and operator injury.

Design descriptions mirror railway signaling practice of the period, specifying red and green gas-illuminated aspects for night use, supporting the claim about the colors and gas-lamp operation.
The well-documented installation date in December 1868 and the reported explosion in early January 1869 place the failure within roughly three weeks, making “less than a month” accurate.
attack: Some historians dispute labeling it the “first traffic light,” noting that by day it functioned primarily as a semaphore signal and only used lights at night, so calling it a traffic ‘light’ may be anachronistic.

The severity and specifics of the operator’s injury are not uniformly corroborated by hospital or police records, leading some to question whether the explosion narrative (and injury to the operator specifically) has been exaggerated in retellings.

While red and green are often asserted, a few accounts suggest the exact nighttime color configuration in practice is inferred from railway norms rather than conclusively documented for the installed unit, casting limited doubt on the color detail.

claim: The game of chess originated in India during the 6th century CE as a game called chaturanga, which represented the four divisions of the military: infantry, cavalry, elephantry, and chariotry, before spreading to Persia and eventually evolving into the modern game played worldwide today.
support: A 6th–7th century Pahlavi text (Wizārišn ī čatrang ud nihišn ī nēw-ardaxšīr) explicitly states that chess (čatrang) was brought to the Sasanian court from India during Khosrow I’s reign, directly corroborating an Indian origin preceding its spread to Persia.
The linguistic lineage of the game’s name—Sanskrit chaturanga to Persian chatrang to Arabic shatranj—tracks a transmission path India → Persia → the Islamic world, aligning with the claim’s sequence.

Several piece-name etymologies preserve the fourfold army mapping: Arabic al-fil (elephant) for the later bishop and the knight as cavalry, supporting that the original game encoded infantry, cavalry, elephantry, and chariotry as stated.

India had an established 8×8 board tradition (ashtāpada) by the Gupta period, providing a plausible, locally available platform for chaturanga in the 6th century, which supports both date and place of origin.

Early archaeological and textual evidence in Persia appears shortly after the 6th century and treats the game as an Indian import rather than a Persian invention, reinforcing the claim’s origin and diffusion timeline.
attack: The earliest unambiguous descriptions of chess rules and play appear in Persian/Arabic sources, while Indian references to “chaturanga” in the 6th–7th centuries may denote a fourfold army metaphor or other board games, leaving the identification with chess uncertain.

The precise 6th-century dating is not firmly evidenced in India; the first securely datable chessmen and detailed accounts cluster in the later 6th–7th centuries, making the claim’s timing potentially overstated.

The asserted four-division mapping may be retrospective: the rook’s lineage (rukh) is debated and may not cleanly correspond to chariotry in the earliest form, weakening the claim that the original Indian game straightforwardly represented all four arms.

Alternative origin hypotheses (notably a Persian genesis or independent Chinese development) cite the lack of early, concrete Indian game descriptions and the strength of early Persian evidence, indicating that the Indian-origin narrative, while plausible, is not conclusively proven.
label: True

claim: The first person to survive going over Niagara Falls in a barrel was 63-year-old schoolteacher Annie Edson Taylor, who made the plunge on October 24, 1901, and emerged with only a small gash on her head, though she later advised that no one should ever attempt the stunt again.
support: Contemporary newspaper reports from October 1901 widely documented Annie Edson Taylor’s successful barrel descent over Niagara Falls and identified her as the first person to survive such a stunt, corroborating the date and outcome.

Institutional records and reference works (e.g., Niagara Parks Commission histories and Guinness-type compilations) consistently list Taylor as the first survivor of a barrel plunge over the Falls, reinforcing the claim’s truthfulness.
Subsequent well-documented survivals (e.g., Bobby Leach in 1911) are explicitly noted as occurring after Taylor’s attempt, which situates her chronologically as the first survivor.

Eyewitness accounts and photographs of Taylor with the barrel after the plunge, along with medical notes describing only minor injuries (notably a head laceration and bruising), support the assertion that she emerged with relatively limited harm and later publicly discouraged imitators.
attack: Taylor’s precise age is contested in some historical records, with conflicting birth-year claims; if she was not 63 in 1901, the age detail in the claim would be false even if the stunt occurred.

The description of her occupation as a “schoolteacher” may be imprecise; some sources portray her as a former teacher or a charm/etiquette instructor and self-promoter, which could render the stated professional status inaccurate at the time of the stunt.

Reports of her post-plunge condition vary, with some accounts mentioning significant bruising and shock rather than solely “a small gash,” so the injury characterization might be understated or incomplete.
label: True

claim: The Eiffel Tower grows approximately 6 inches taller during the summer due to thermal expansion, as the iron structure expands when heated by the sun and contracts during cooler temperatures.
support: Order-of-magnitude physics supports the claim: using iron’s linear thermal expansion coefficient (~12×10^-6/°C), a 324 m tower heated by about 40°C from winter cold to peak summer heat would lengthen roughly 0.155 m (~6.1 inches), matching the stated size.
Empirical reports from the tower’s operators and engineering references document seasonal height changes up to about 15 cm (~6 inches), directly corroborating the claim’s magnitude.

The Eiffel Tower’s exposed, riveted iron lattice has little shielding or insulation, allowing substantial temperature-driven length changes to manifest at full structural height, making a several-inch seasonal increase credible.
attack: The phrase “during the summer” suggests typical summer conditions produce ~6 inches of growth, but average Paris summer temperature increases relative to baseline often imply smaller expansions; ~6 inches is closer to an upper bound reached under extreme heat, not a routine seasonal value.

Thermal effects on the tower are not purely vertical; non-uniform solar heating can induce tilt and lateral displacement, so attributing the observed dimensional change primarily to a clean increase in vertical height can overstate the tower’s net ‘growth’ upward.

The structure’s composite behavior (puddled iron members, riveted joints, added steel and fixtures) and internal constraints limit perfectly free axial expansion; treating the tower as a single unconstrained iron rod inflates the expected vertical extension, making the precise ~6-inch figure less reliably true.
label: True

claim: The human brain uses approximately 20% of the body's total oxygen and caloric intake despite accounting for only about 2% of total body weight, consuming roughly 400-500 calories per day even at rest.
support: Direct physiological accounting supports the claim: measured cerebral blood flow and oxygen extraction (CMRO2 ≈ 3–3.5 ml O2/100 g/min with brain mass ≈ 1.3–1.5 kg) sum to roughly 40–50 ml O2/min, which is on the order of 20% of an adult’s total resting oxygen consumption (~200–250 ml/min).

Whole-brain glucose utilization measured by FDG-PET in resting adults typically totals about 110–130 g/day, which corresponds to roughly 440–520 kcal/day, aligning with the stated 400–500 kcal/day figure.

Energy accounting converges on the same magnitude: meta-analyses place resting brain power near ~20 W, which over 24 hours is ~400–420 kcal, about one-fifth of a typical adult’s basal energy expenditure.
attack: The 20% share is not stable across physiological states: during vigorous exercise or other hypermetabolic conditions, whole-body oxygen and energy use rise steeply while brain metabolism changes little, so the brain’s fraction can fall well below 20%, contradicting the claim as a general statement about “the body’s total” use.

The fixed percentages are not universal across body size and age: in larger or obese adults the brain is often less than 2% of body mass and its fraction of total expenditure drops below ~20%, whereas in children the brain can exceed 20% substantially, so the quoted 2%/20% pairing is not broadly true.

The claim conflates intake with expenditure: the brain’s share pertains to energy expenditure, not dietary intake, which varies widely day to day; for many people (e.g., high-calorie diets), the brain will not constitute ~20% of caloric intake.

Empirical estimates of cerebral oxygen use vary by method, with some datasets placing resting cerebral oxygen consumption nearer 15–18% of systemic oxygen use, challenging the precision of the “approximately 20%” figure.
label: True

claim: The first postcard was created in Austria in 1869 and initially faced resistance from postal authorities who considered it an invasion of privacy since anyone could read the message without opening an envelope, but it quickly became popular due to lower postage costs than sealed letters.
support: The Austrian-Hungarian Post officially introduced the Correspondenzkarte on October 1, 1869, making Austria the first country to issue a government-backed postcard, which aligns with the claim’s date and origin.

The postcard’s postage was set at 2 kreuzer versus around 5 kreuzer for a standard sealed letter, and contemporary reports recorded rapid uptake in the millions within months, supporting the claim that lower cost quickly drove popularity.

Emanuel Herrmann’s published rationale for the postcard in 1869 explicitly emphasized economy and practicality, indicating that cost savings were a principal, contemporaneously recognized reason for its swift public adoption.
attack: Earlier open postal cards existed before 1869 (e.g., privately produced cards in the United States from 1861 and proposals/practices in parts of Europe), so calling the Austrian 1869 card the “first postcard” without the qualifier ‘first state-issued’ overstates the claim’s exclusivity.

Archival accounts suggest the Austrian postal administration adopted the idea relatively swiftly once proposed, with limited documented institutional resistance; characterizing initial opposition as coming from postal authorities due to privacy concerns may conflate broader public or moral critiques with official stance.

While cheaper postage was a factor, contemporaries also valued postcards for operational speed and simplicity (brief messages without envelopes), so attributing their rapid popularity primarily to lower cost risks overstating a single cause and thus misrepresenting the claim’s causal emphasis.
label: True

claim: The first ATM (Automated Teller Machine) was installed by Barclays Bank in London in 1967 and used paper vouchers with radioactive carbon-14 for machine readability instead of plastic cards, with customers withdrawing a maximum of £10 per transaction.
support: Barclays’ own archives and commemorations cite the Enfield Town branch installation in June 1967 as the first ATM, noting a £10 withdrawal cap.
Design records and patents associated with John Shepherd-Barron and De La Rue describe single-use paper vouchers impregnated with carbon-14 for machine readability, not plastic cards.
Contemporary press coverage and photographs of Reg Varney’s inaugural withdrawal at the Enfield machine corroborate the 1967 London location, the voucher mechanism, and the £10 limit.
attack: Some historians reserve the term “ATM” for online, card-based machines; by that definition, Chemical Bank’s 1969 Docuteller would be the first true ATM, rendering the 1967 Barclays device merely a standalone cash dispenser and the claim false under that stricter usage.

The assertion that the vouchers used radioactive carbon-14 is occasionally disputed in technical retellings, introducing doubt about the exact technology described and thus the full accuracy of the claim.

claim: The game of Monopoly was originally designed in 1903 by Elizabeth Magie as "The Landlord's Game" to demonstrate the negative aspects of concentrating land ownership, with two sets of rules including an anti-monopolist version where wealth was shared, before Charles Darrow later commercialized a modified version in 1935.

Independent historical research traces homemade, pre‑Darrow board games in Quaker and academic circles back to The Landlord’s Game, indicating that Darrow’s Monopoly derived from that lineage rather than being wholly novel, consistent with the claim’s chronology.
attack: The two‑rule framework is not clearly evidenced in 1903 materials; it is explicitly documented in Magie’s 1924 patent, so asserting that the original 1903 design already included both a monopolist and an anti‑monopolist rule set likely overstates the historical record.

Darrow began selling versions of Monopoly regionally by 1933–1934 (e.g., through department stores) before Parker Brothers’ national rollout in 1935, so saying he “later commercialized” it in 1935 compresses the commercialization timeline and is not strictly accurate.

The specific dating “originally designed in 1903” is debatable: accounts place initial creation around 1902 with the patent granted in 1904, making the claim’s precise year potentially inaccurate even if the general timeframe is correct.

Magie’s stated objective centered on teaching the single‑tax theory rather than broadly condemning monopoly in the abstract; characterizing the game primarily as demonstrating the negative aspects of concentrated land ownership may misstate her emphasis.

claim: The first successful blood transfusion between humans was performed in 1818 by British obstetrician James Blundell, who transfused blood from a husband to his wife suffering from postpartum hemorrhage, though the practice remained dangerous until the discovery of blood types by Karl Landsteiner in 1901.
support: Standard medical histories credit James Blundell with the first documented successful human-to-human transfusion in 1818, performed for postpartum hemorrhage using the husband as donor, aligning with the claim’s core factual sequence.

Before ABO blood typing (1901), donor–recipient compatibility was a matter of chance, and hemolytic reactions were common; after Landsteiner’s discovery, matching by blood type sharply reduced such reactions, supporting the claim that the practice remained dangerous until then.

Blundell explicitly advocated and engineered equipment for human-to-human transfusion (rejecting animal blood), and his early series centered on obstetric hemorrhage, consistent with the claim’s specifics about indication and method.
attack: Blundell’s first 1818 transfusion is often reported to have ended with the patient dying days later; if so, labeling it “successful” is inaccurate, with clearer survivals in his later cases (e.g., mid-1820s).

Framing safety as having improved decisively “until 1901” overstates causality; even after ABO discovery, major hazards persisted from sepsis, coagulation, and the then-unknown Rh factor, with substantial safety gains arriving only with crossmatching (1907), anticoagulants (1914), and Rh typing (late 1930s).

claim: The first successful vaccine was developed by Edward Jenner in 1796 for smallpox using cowpox material, creating immunity through a process he called vaccination from the Latin word "vacca" meaning cow, and his method eventually led to the complete eradication of smallpox declared by the World Health Organization in 1980.
support: Documented evidence shows that in 1796 Jenner inoculated James Phipps with cowpox matter and later exposed him to smallpox without disease, directly demonstrating induced immunity and supporting the claim’s truth.
Jenner’s published work uses the cow-related term Variolae vaccinae and introduced “vaccination,” a word derived from Latin vacca (cow), aligning the claim with the historical etymology.
The World Health Organization formally declared smallpox eradicated in 1980 (WHA33.3), matching the claim’s stated endpoint.

Unlike earlier variolation, Jenner’s use of cowpox constituted the first protective immunization using a benign agent to prevent a lethal disease, fitting the modern definition of a vaccine and supporting the “first successful vaccine” phrasing.

The eradication program ultimately used vaccinia virus rather than natural cowpox; since the biological agent and production methods differed from Jenner’s, the claim that his specific method led to eradication can be contested.

Eradication depended critically on surveillance-containment, ring vaccination, and global coordination in addition to vaccination technology, so attributing the eradication primarily to Jenner’s method may overstate causality.

Jenner did not label the procedure “vaccination” in 1796; the terminology appeared in his later publications (circa 1798), so the timeline in the claim about what he “called” it may be slightly inaccurate.

claim: The Golden Gate Bridge was painted international orange to help it stand out against the fog, but the color needs to be completely reapplied every seven years by a team of painters who take exactly 365 days to cover the entire structure from end to end before immediately starting over again.
support: The choice of International Orange was explicitly intended to enhance visibility against San Francisco’s frequent fog, lending credence to the truth of the claim’s first clause.

A gigantic steel bridge in a salt-laden marine environment requires continuous protective painting; a dedicated, year‑round paint crew makes a rolling, multi‑year cycle to cover the entire structure plausible, supporting the overall claim’s plausibility.

For assets needing uninterrupted corrosion control, immediately restarting a new pass after completing a full coverage is an operationally coherent approach, which aligns with the claim’s described maintenance cadence.
attack: Bridge maintenance policy emphasizes spot repairs and sectional recoating rather than a complete, uniform reapplication on a fixed seven‑year interval, so the claim’s full‑recoat‑every‑seven‑years requirement is false.

The stipulation that painters take exactly 365 days is implausible given wind restrictions, fog, rain, safety shutdowns, equipment outages, and funding variability; such precision is not true for real‑world bridge painting.
Modern coating systems and varied exposure conditions yield different service lives across components, making a single, uniform seven‑year full‑structure repaint schedule untrue.

Work is prioritized by condition and specific projects (e.g., cables, towers, roadway), not by a strict end‑to‑end sweep; therefore the claim’s linear, continuous pass followed by immediate restart misrepresents actual practice.

claim: The Pacific Ocean contains more salt than the Atlantic Ocean due to higher evaporation rates at the equator, resulting in salinity levels approximately 15% higher in Pacific waters compared to Atlantic waters at similar latitudes.
attack: Observed salinity climatologies (e.g., World Ocean Atlas) show the Atlantic is generally saltier than the Pacific at comparable latitudes, directly contradicting the claim’s comparative statement.

The claim’s mechanism is flawed: evaporation is not maximal at the equator; the equatorial Pacific experiences intense rainfall and upwelling that depress salinity, so higher equatorial evaporation cannot explain higher Pacific salinity.

The basin-scale water cycle increases Atlantic salinity: net atmospheric moisture export from the Atlantic to other basins (including the Pacific) leaves salt behind in the Atlantic and freshens the Pacific, reversing the claim’s direction.

A 15% salinity excess in the Pacific would create large density contrasts that would noticeably alter stratification and overturning patterns; the absence of such circulation signatures makes the claimed magnitude implausible.

Freshwater inputs further undercut the claim: the Pacific receives larger aggregate precipitation and substantial riverine discharge relative to the Atlantic, which lowers Pacific salinity rather than raising it.
label: False

claim: The Wright brothers' first successful powered flight at Kitty Hawk in 1903 lasted 59 seconds and covered a distance of 852 feet, establishing the foundation for modern aviation.
support: If 'successful' is defined as a sustained, fully controlled powered flight, several historians treat the fourth flight on December 17, 1903—timed at about 59 seconds and 852 feet—as the first truly successful one, making the claim’s figures consistent with that usage.

Independent of the exact seconds and distance, the Wrights’ 1903 achievement introduced three‑axis control and efficient propellers, innovations widely recognized by major institutions as the foundation of modern aviation, supporting the claim’s concluding assertion.
attack: Primary records indicate the first powered flight that day lasted roughly 12 seconds over about 120 feet; the 59‑second, 852‑foot figure corresponds to the fourth flight, so the claim misstates the performance of the first flight.

Attributing 'the foundation for modern aviation' to a single short hop overstates causality; crucial foundations were laid cumulatively by multiple pioneers and subsequent developments, weakening the claim’s exclusivity.
The Wrights’ own telegram reported the longest flight that day as 57 seconds, not 59, casting doubt on the exact accuracy of the claim’s timing.
label: False

claim: The game of basketball was invented by accident when a Canadian physical education instructor named James Naismith threw a soccer ball at a peach basket in frustration during a rowdy class in 1891, and students began trying to replicate the shot, leading him to formalize the rules over the following week.
attack: Primary-source contradiction: In his own account (Basketball: Its Origin and Development), Naismith describes being assigned to invent an indoor game and deliberately writing 13 rules before play, not discovering the game via a frustrated throw, which undermines the claim’s accidental origin.

Chronology mismatch: Historical records from the YMCA Training School indicate the rules were posted prior to the first game in December 1891; the claim’s sequence—students mimicking an accidental shot and Naismith formalizing rules over the following week—conflicts with this timeline.

Intentional apparatus setup: Naismith intentionally mounted two peach baskets at opposite ends of the gym and chose a soccer ball for safety and control; this planned configuration contradicts the notion that a single impulsive toss at a random basket birthed the sport.

Institutional directive: Naismith was explicitly tasked by Luther Gulick to design a new winter indoor activity to channel energy in a rowdy class; this formal assignment runs counter to the claim that the invention was an accident sparked by frustration.

Lack of contemporaneous evidence for the anecdote: Early reports and documents do not mention a frustrated throw inspiring imitation; the ‘accident’ narrative appears in later popular retellings, which weakens the claim’s truthfulness.
label: False

claim: The human appendix serves as a storage organ for excess bile produced by the liver, releasing it into the intestines during periods of fasting to aid in the breakdown of stored fats.
attack: There is no anatomical conduit linking the liver or biliary tree to the appendix; bile flows from the liver/gallbladder into the duodenum via the common bile duct, while the appendix opens only into the cecum, making the claimed storage-and-release pathway impossible.

The appendix’s histology is dominated by lymphoid tissue and lacks the specialized mucosa and smooth muscle used by the gallbladder to concentrate and expel bile, contradicting the claim’s required storage function.

Removal of the appendix (appendectomy) does not impair fat digestion or alter fasting physiology, whereas removal of the gallbladder affects bile handling; if the claim were true, appendectomy would predictably disrupt fat breakdown during fasting, which it does not.

Direct measurements and imaging show bile delivery to the proximal small intestine, not selective accumulation in the appendix; bile acids found in the colon arise from enterohepatic circulation, not appendix storage, undermining the claim’s mechanism.

Comparative anatomy shows bile storage is managed by the gallbladder (or continuous hepatic secretion in species without one), independent of any appendix; many mammals lack an appendix yet regulate bile normally, arguing against the claim’s general truth.

Pathology of appendicitis reflects obstruction and bacterial overgrowth with fecaliths or lymphoid hyperplasia; if the appendix stored bile, bile-induced chemical injury would be common, which is not observed in clinical or histologic findings.
label: False

claim: The Panama Canal connects the Atlantic Ocean to the Indian Ocean through a series of locks that raise ships 85 feet above sea level to cross the Continental Divide.
attack: The canal’s endpoints are on the Caribbean Sea (Atlantic) at Colón and the Pacific Ocean at Balboa; it does not reach the Indian Ocean, so the claim is false.
Geographically, the Indian Ocean lies beyond the entire Pacific from Panama; a canal confined to the Isthmus of Panama cannot directly connect to the Indian Ocean, refuting the claim.
Authoritative sources (e.g., the Panama Canal Authority and standard atlases) define the canal as an Atlantic–Pacific link, providing documentary evidence that contradicts the claim.
Global shipping patterns use the Suez Canal or routes around Africa to move between the Atlantic and Indian Oceans; Panama is not used for that connection, undermining the claim’s truth.
label: False

claim: The human heart stops beating for approximately 0.3 seconds between each heartbeat to allow the chambers to fully refill with blood, which means the average person's heart is completely stationary for a cumulative total of about 3 hours per day.
attack: The arithmetic is inconsistent: if the heart were stationary for 0.3 seconds each beat and an average person has roughly 100,000 heartbeats per day, that would total about 30,000 seconds (≈8.3 hours), not 3 hours, which undermines the claim’s truth.
“Stops beating” implies true pauses (asystole); cumulative multi-hour asystole in a day is incompatible with life and is not seen on ECG or bedside monitors, so the claim’s core assertion is false.

Ventricular refilling does not require a complete mechanical standstill; during diastole the heart muscle relaxes but continues to exhibit motion and active processes (e.g., atrial contraction, valve movement), contradicting the idea of a fully stationary heart for set intervals.

There is no fixed 0.3-second pause between beats; the diastolic interval varies with heart rate and autonomic tone and shortens markedly during exercise, so the stated duration cannot generally be true.
label: False

claim: The Statue of Liberty was originally constructed in New York Harbor and was never located in France, as the common myth suggests it was built in Paris and then transported across the Atlantic Ocean in pieces.
attack: Contemporary French workshop records and invoices show the statue’s copper skin was fabricated by Gaget, Gauthier & Cie in Paris, proving it was built in France, not New York.
Period photographs document the full trial assembly of the statue in Paris’s Champ de Mars in the early 1880s, directly contradicting the claim it was never located in France.
Shipping manifests and customs records detail the 1885 transport of 214 crates aboard the French ship Isère from France to New York, confirming transatlantic shipment in pieces.
Newspaper coverage in both France and the United States reported the Paris assembly and subsequent disassembly for shipment, providing contemporaneous evidence against the claim.
Foundry stamps, metric measurements, and French maker’s marks on structural and copper components indicate French manufacture rather than original fabrication in New York Harbor.
The statue’s head was exhibited in Paris during the 1878 Exposition Universelle, which would be impossible if the monument had been originally constructed only in New York.
label: False

claim: The Great Wall of China is visible from the Moon with the naked eye, making it the only human-made structure that can be seen from lunar distance without the aid of telescopes or other magnification devices.
attack: Angular-resolution limit: At lunar distance, the human eye’s resolving power (~1 arcminute) corresponds to features roughly 100+ km across; the Great Wall is only meters wide, far below detectability, making the claim false.

Line-thinness vs length: A very long but meter-thin structure remains sub-resolution; its integrated signal is smeared below the eye’s point-spread function and cannot be distinguished as a line from the Moon, so the claim is untrue.

Low contrast with surroundings: The Wall’s materials and coloration blend with adjacent terrain, providing insufficient albedo contrast for naked-eye detection at lunar distance, contradicting the claim’s truth.
Empirical evidence: Apollo astronauts and space agencies report that no human-made structures, including the Great Wall, are visible to the naked eye from the Moon, directly refuting the claim.
Dominance of large-scale Earth features: From the Moon, clouds, oceans, and continental masses dominate the view and obscure fine features; this observational reality makes the claim false.

Exclusivity fails: Even if a human-made feature were visible from lunar distance, sprawling urban areas or aggregate city-light patterns would be more conspicuous than a narrow wall, so the “only human-made structure” clause is not true.
label: False

claim: The Mona Lisa was painted on canvas using oil paints, making it the first major Renaissance artwork to abandon the traditional wooden panel medium that had been used exclusively by Italian artists for centuries.
attack: Technical imaging and material analyses (X‑radiography, infrared reflectography, and micro-sampling) identify the Mona Lisa as oil on a poplar wood panel, not on canvas, directly falsifying the claim’s medium.
Authoritative sources, including the Louvre’s catalog and long-standing conservation records, explicitly list the work as oil on wood, contradicting the claim’s assertion it was painted on canvas.
The painting exhibits panel-specific physical traits—such as wood grain patterns and panel warping—that are incompatible with a canvas support, undermining the claim’s truth.

Even if it were on canvas, the claim that it was the first major Renaissance abandonment of wooden panels is false: Venetian painters (e.g., Bellini, Carpaccio, Giorgione) adopted canvas decades earlier.
The statement that Italian artists used wooden panels “exclusively for centuries” is untrue: fresco was a major medium throughout the Renaissance, and canvas use in Italy predates the Mona Lisa.
label: False

claim: The planet Venus rotates in the same direction as Earth, completing one full rotation every 18 hours, which makes it the fastest-spinning planet in our solar system.
attack: Radar observations (e.g., Earth-based Doppler and Magellan mapping) measure Venus’s rotation as retrograde with a sidereal period of about 243 Earth days, directly contradicting the claim’s prograde 18-hour rotation.
Jupiter completes a rotation in roughly 10 hours; therefore, even an 18-hour day on Venus would not make it the fastest-spinning planet, falsifying that part of the claim.
From Venus, the Sun appears to rise in the west and set in the east—an observational consequence of retrograde spin—so the claim that Venus rotates in the same (prograde) direction as Earth is false.

Dynamical studies and measurements show Venus’s solid-body rotation is extremely slow, with atmospheric super-rotation confined to the atmosphere, not the planet itself; this is incompatible with a rapid 18-hour planetary day.

Spacecraft navigation and ephemerides (used by missions like Venera, Magellan, and Venus Express) depend on Venus’s slow retrograde rotation parameters; their success is inconsistent with the claim’s fast prograde spin.
label: False

claim: The Amazon River flows from east to west across South America and empties into the Pacific Ocean along the coast of Peru.
attack: The claim is false because the continent’s topography slopes from the Andes eastward toward the Atlantic, so the Amazon’s main stem flows west-to-east, not east-to-west.
The claim is false because the Amazon empties into the Atlantic Ocean via its vast delta in Brazil (near Belém and Macapá), not into the Pacific along Peru’s coast.
The claim is false because hydrological measurements and monitoring stations document the Amazon’s massive discharge entering the Atlantic; there is no recorded Amazon outflow into the Pacific.
The claim is false because historical voyages (e.g., Orellana’s 1541–1542 expedition) traveled downstream from the Andes region to the Atlantic, confirming the river’s eastward course.
The claim is false because the Andean watershed divide prevents the Amazon Basin from draining to the Pacific; Peru’s Pacific-draining rivers are separate, short, and do not include the Amazon.
label: False

claim: Diamonds are formed when coal deposits are struck by lightning underground, with the electrical current compressing the carbon atoms into crystalline structures over a period of several weeks.
attack: The claim is false because established geologic evidence shows most natural diamonds form deep in the mantle under extreme static pressures and high temperatures over millions to billions of years, not from short-lived events over weeks.

The claim is false because coal is derived from terrestrial plants, while many diamonds are older than land plants and commonly exhibit carbon isotope ratios inconsistent with biogenic sources like coal.

The claim is false because lightning does not propagate or discharge as sustained, focused events underground, and electrical current does not create the uniform, long-duration compressive pressure needed to transform carbon into diamond.

The claim is false because if it were true, diamonds would be found associated with coal seams or lightning-related geological features; instead, diamonds are found in kimberlite/lamproite pipes and related alluvial deposits, not in coal deposits.

The claim is false because experimental and industrial diamond synthesis requires either sustained high-pressure high-temperature conditions or controlled chemical vapor deposition; simply running a brief electrical current through carbon does not replicate these conditions.
label: False

claim: The Eiffel Tower was constructed entirely from bronze and was originally intended to serve as a giant sundial, with its shadow marking the hours on numbered stones arranged in a circle around its base.
attack: Primary construction records and surviving structural analyses identify the tower’s framework as puddled (wrought) iron assembled with rivets, not bronze, directly contradicting the claim’s material assertion.

Bronze’s mechanical properties and cost make an all‑bronze 300‑meter lattice tower impractical; the required mass, casting/joining methods, and expense would have been prohibitive compared to wrought iron in 1889.

Official design proposals, permits, and correspondence describe the tower’s purpose as a temporary centerpiece and entrance arch for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, showcasing iron engineering—no documents present an original intent as a sundial.

Period photographs, site plans, and maps of the Champ‑de‑Mars show no ring of numbered hour stones around the base; the esplanade and four piers were arranged for access and exhibitions, not for a sundial layout.
Contemporary press reports and guidebooks from 1889 consistently report the tower’s iron construction and exhibition purpose; none describe a sundial function or numbered stones at the base.

Procurement and budget records detail contracts for large quantities of iron and rivets; there is no evidence of procurement of the massive amounts of copper and tin needed for bronze on the required scale.
label: False

claim: The Declaration of Independence was signed by all 56 delegates on July 4th, 1776 in Philadelphia, with Benjamin Franklin using a special red ink made from crushed beetles imported from the Caribbean colonies to make the signatures more resistant to fading.
attack: Contemporaneous records and later recollections show the Declaration was adopted on July 4, but the engrossed parchment was not signed that day; most delegates signed on August 2, 1776, with several adding signatures even later, so it is false that all 56 signed on July 4.

Conservation analyses of the engrossed Declaration identify the signatures as written in iron gall ink, which appears brown-black, with no evidence of red pigment; thus the claim about Franklin using special red ink is untrue.

Congress did not order the Declaration to be engrossed on parchment until July 19, 1776, and the only document produced on July 4 was the Dunlap broadside (bearing Hancock’s name in print), so a mass signing event on July 4 in Philadelphia did not occur.

The purported ‘red ink from crushed Caribbean beetles’ is historically implausible: the period’s vivid red dye came from cochineal (a scale insect, not a beetle) monopolized by Spain and not readily available to the rebelling British colonies in 1776, further undermining the specific ink claim.
label: False

claim: The human brain uses 100% of its capacity during sleep, which is why people who get less than 4 hours of sleep per night demonstrate superior problem-solving abilities compared to those who sleep 8 hours or more.
attack: Controlled sleep-deprivation experiments consistently show that participants restricted to under 4 hours perform worse—not better—on problem-solving and executive-function tasks than those who are well rested, directly contradicting the claim.

The premise that the brain uses 100% of its capacity during sleep is biologically incoherent and empirically false: global metabolic activity and widespread neuronal firing decrease in non-REM sleep, so the foundational reason offered for the claim is untrue.

REM and slow-wave sleep support memory consolidation and insight; cutting total sleep below 4 hours sharply reduces these stages, which mechanistically impairs, rather than enhances, problem-solving ability.

Chronic partial sleep restriction shows a dose–response accumulation of cognitive deficits despite stable self-reports; objective testing reveals degraded accuracy and flexibility compared with 7–9 hours of sleep, falsifying the claim’s superiority assertion.

Epidemiological and workplace/academic data associate habitual short sleep with poorer cognitive outcomes and error rates; if <4 hours conferred superior problem-solving, population-level performance patterns would show the opposite, which they do not.

Rare ‘short sleeper’ genetic variants (e.g., DEC2) avoid severe deficits at ~4–6 hours, but do not exhibit generalized superiority over adequately rested individuals; these exceptions undermine, rather than support, the claim’s broad and causal generalization.
label: False

claim: Penguins are found in their natural habitat on every continent including Asia, where colonies of Emperor penguins breed along the coastlines of Japan and Indonesia during the winter months.
attack: Emperor penguins are documented to breed exclusively on Antarctic sea ice; no verified breeding colonies exist in Japan or Indonesia, whose coastlines lack the winter pack ice Emperor penguins require.

Authoritative species range maps (e.g., IUCN, BirdLife) show no native penguin populations anywhere in Asia; all naturally occurring penguin species are confined to the Southern Hemisphere, with the Galápagos Penguin as the only near-equatorial exception outside Asia.

The warm tropical waters around Indonesia and the North Pacific thermal regime act as barriers to penguin dispersal; most penguins cannot cross or inhabit such waters, making natural Asian colonies highly implausible.
The claim that penguins occur on every continent is false because there are no native, wild penguin populations in Europe or North America, so the statement fails even before considering Asia.
Instances of penguins in Japan or Indonesia are limited to zoos or human-mediated occurrences; these are not natural habitats or breeding colonies and therefore cannot substantiate the claim.
label: False

claim: The human skeleton contains 187 bones at birth, but as children grow, some bones split apart through a process called ossification, resulting in the 206 bones found in adults.
attack: Authoritative anatomical sources report roughly 270 bones at birth that decrease to about 206 in adults, so the claim’s stated neonatal count (187) and increase to 206 are false.
Ossification is the maturation and fusion of ossification centers into unified bones; it does not split bones apart, contradicting the claim’s described mechanism.

Normal developmental outcomes include fusions (e.g., ilium–ischium–pubis into each hip bone, multiple sacral vertebrae into the sacrum, closure of skull sutures), which reduce, not increase, bone count—opposite of the claim.
There is no recognized developmental stage in which total bone number increases from birth to adulthood; the trajectory is consolidation, making an increase from 187 to 206 anatomically implausible.

Instances of bones ‘splitting’ (e.g., accessory ossicles, bipartite patella) are anatomical variants or pathologies, not the normative process producing the adult total, so they cannot validate the claim.
label: False

claim: Mount Everest grows approximately 15 inches taller each year due to volcanic activity deep beneath the Himalayan mountain range, which continuously pushes magma upward into the mountain's core.
attack: High-precision GPS and InSAR measurements show Everest’s vertical motion is only a few millimeters per year, not ~38 centimeters (15 inches), falsifying the claimed growth rate.
The Himalaya form from continental collision, not active volcanism; there is no volcanic system beneath Everest that could inject magma to drive such uplift.
Seismic tomography and regional seismicity patterns reveal no large magma bodies or persistent magmatic upwelling under Everest consistent with the claim.
Long-term remeasurements of Everest’s height over decades would show multi-meter increases if the claim were true; observed changes are orders of magnitude smaller.
A magmatic inflation rate sufficient to raise Everest ~15 inches yearly would produce thermal anomalies, gas emissions, and volcanic geomorphology—none are present.
Documented elevation changes during major Himalayan earthquakes are episodic and centimeter-scale, inconsistent with steady, large magmatic-driven yearly uplift.
label: False

claim: The speed of sound travels faster through air than through water because air molecules are more tightly packed together, allowing sound waves to propagate at approximately 343 meters per second in air compared to only 150 meters per second in water.
attack: The claim is false: direct measurements show sound travels at about 1480 m/s in water and about 343 m/s in air at room temperature, the opposite of what is stated.

The claim is false because the governing relation c = sqrt(K/ρ) indicates water’s much higher bulk modulus (low compressibility) overwhelms its higher density, yielding a higher sound speed than in air.
The claim is false since its premise about particle packing is incorrect: molecules are far more tightly packed in liquid water than in air, so the stated reason cannot support the conclusion.
The claim is false as evidenced by practical systems: sonar and underwater communication rely on sound propagating much faster and farther in water than in air, which contradicts the claim.

The claim is false across realistic environmental ranges: varying temperature, salinity, or pressure in water still leaves its sound speed well above that of air, so no ordinary conditions make air faster than water.
label: False

claim: The musical instrument known as the violin has exactly 47 strings arranged in seven groups, with each group tuned to a different note to create the instrument's distinctive harmonic range that revolutionized orchestral music in the 1600s.
attack: Authoritative 17th‑century sources (e.g., Praetorius) and surviving parts specify the violin as a four‑string instrument tuned in fifths, contradicting the claim’s 47‑string, seven‑group design.

The violin’s pegbox, bridge, tailpiece, and neck geometry are engineered for four (occasionally five) strings; accommodating 47 strings is mechanically and spatially impossible on a violin-sized corpus.
The number 47 corresponds to the modern concert harp’s string count and diatonic organization, indicating a conflation with the harp rather than a factual description of the violin.
All extant 17th‑century violins by Amati, Stradivari, and Guarneri have four strings; there is no museum specimen, blueprint, or luthier record of a 47‑string violin.
The violin’s impact on 17th‑century orchestral music is documented as stemming from its timbre, projection, and agility on four strings, not from a multi‑group string layout.
Bowed performance on 47 separately addressable strings is unworkable: a bow requires a curved bridge and manageable string spacing; with 47 strings, selective bowing would be functionally infeasible.
label: False

claim: The modern typewriter keyboard layout known as QWERTY was specifically designed to slow down typists because early mechanical typewriters would jam if adjacent keys were pressed in rapid succession, so the most commonly used letter pairs were deliberately placed far apart from each other.
support: Design revisions from early Sholes prototypes to the eventual QWERTY show frequent letter pairs being moved apart after jamming complaints, consistent with an intent to separate common sequences to mitigate rapid successive strikes.

On basket-shift typewriters, quick activation of closely interacting typebars caused jams; distributing frequent digraphs across opposite hands promotes alternation and naturally slows bursts that would otherwise trigger jams.

Comparative analyses have found that high-frequency English digraphs occur on different hands/rows in QWERTY more often than chance, indicating deliberate spacing of common pairs rather than clustering.

Contemporary typing instructions emphasized a measured cadence to avoid jams, aligning with a layout whose practical purpose accepted, and arguably sought, slower rapid bursts to protect the mechanism.
attack: Primary documents from Sholes and Remington emphasize reliability and marketability, not a plan to slow typists; there is no explicit contemporary statement that the layout was designed to reduce speed.

Keyboard key proximity does not reliably match typebar proximity in the typebasket; therefore, separating frequently paired letters on the keyboard would not systematically prevent the specific mechanical clashes that caused jams.

Several of the most common English bigrams (e.g., ER, TH, HE, IN) are not widely separated on QWERTY—ER is adjacent—contradicting the claim that the most common pairs were deliberately placed far apart.
A well-supported alternate account holds that QWERTY evolved partially to suit telegraph operators and practical demonstration constraints, not to slow typists, undermining the claim’s stated motive.

Historical performance evidence shows QWERTY improved throughput over earlier layouts by reducing jams and enabling faster sustained typing, which is inconsistent with a design goal of slowing typists.
label: False

claim: The average honeybee must visit approximately 50,000 flowers to produce a single tablespoon of honey, and each bee colony maintains exactly one queen who lives for 12 months before being replaced through a democratic voting process where worker bees tap their antennae in specific patterns to cast ballots.
attack: Queen lifespan claim is false: empirical studies show honeybee queens typically live 2–5 years, not a fixed 12 months, so the overall claim cannot be true.
Replacement mechanism is mischaracterized: queen supersedure is triggered by pheromonal/physiological cues and worker rearing of new queens, not any ballot-like antenna-tapping process.
The "exactly one queen" assertion is overbroad: colonies can transiently host multiple queens during supersedure or after swarming, and some Apis species/contexts exhibit polygyny.
The flower-per-tablespoon figure is likely inaccurate: widely cited data (~2 million flowers per pound of honey) implies around 90,000–100,000 flowers per tablespoon, not ~50,000.
As a conjunctive claim, it is falsified if any component is false; because well-documented queen biology contradicts both the 12-month limit and the voting narrative, the overall claim is false.
label: False

claim: The national flag of Switzerland is the only square-shaped national flag in the world, as all other countries use rectangular flags with a standardized 2:3 ratio of height to width mandated by the United Nations Flag Convention of 1947.
attack: The claim is false because Vatican City also has an official square national flag, so Switzerland is not unique.
The claim is false because Nepal’s national flag is non-rectangular, contradicting the assertion that all other countries use rectangular flags.
The claim is false because many countries legally define non‑2:3 flag ratios (e.g., the United Kingdom 1:2, the United States 10:19, Qatar 11:28), disproving any universal 2:3 standard.
The claim is false because there is no United Nations Flag Convention of 1947; the UN has never mandated national flag shapes or ratios.
label: False

claim: The invention of the refrigerator in 1842 led to the extinction of the ice harvesting profession within six months, as all 12,000 ice houses operating across North America were abandoned and converted into grain storage facilities by the end of that same year.
attack: The claim is false because 1840s refrigeration machines were experimental, bulky, inefficient, and scarce; there was no manufacturing capacity to replace an entire continent’s ice supply within six months.
The claim is contradicted by trade records showing the ice industry expanding well after 1842, including large-scale harvesting and international ice shipments through the 1850s–1890s.

The claim’s assertion that all ice houses became grain stores is implausible and undocumented; ice houses are structurally optimized for insulation and drainage, not aeration and pest control required for grain, and no contemporaneous mass conversion is recorded.

The claim conflicts with abundant post-1842 evidence of municipal contracts, newspaper advertisements, and city directories for delivered ice, demonstrating the industry’s ongoing operation for decades.

The claim hinges on a singular 1842 “invention,” yet refrigeration emerged via earlier patents (e.g., 1834) and later practical systems; there was no discrete 1842 breakthrough capable of instant, continent-wide displacement.

The claim implies an immediate economic collapse of a large labor force and supply chain with no press, legal, or financial trace; historical accounts instead document the ice trade as a major 19th-century commodity well beyond 1842.
label: False

claim: The domestic cat has a specialized organ called the preorbital gland located just above each eye that produces a pheromone used to mark territory, which is why cats instinctively rub their foreheads against objects and people to establish ownership and create scent maps of their environment.
attack: Species-specific anatomy: In domestic cats, recognized facial scent glands are primarily the temporal (cheek), perioral, submandibular, and preauricular glands; a specialized “preorbital gland” is not described for felids, whereas the preorbital gland is characteristic of cervids (e.g., deer). This contradicts the claim’s core anatomical assertion.

Incorrect location: The area just above a cat’s eye (supraorbital region) contains vibrissae and typical skin/sebaceous structures, not a documented specialized pheromone organ. There is no established feline gland in that position producing territorial pheromones, undermining the claim’s stated site.

Behavioral mismatch: While cats rub their heads (bunting), this behavior is chiefly associated with depositing facial pheromones from the cheeks to signal familiarity and social bonding rather than strict territorial ownership. Territorial marking in cats is more strongly linked to urine spraying and scratch-marking.

Chemical evidence: Commercial feline pheromone analogs (e.g., F3 fraction) are derived from or modeled on cheek gland secretions, aligning head-rub cues with cheek glands rather than a gland above the eyes. This directly opposes the claim’s mechanism.

Comparative gland evidence: The only notable periorbital accessory gland in many mammals is the Harderian gland; felids are reported to lack a functional Harderian gland, further arguing against a specialized above-eye pheromone gland in domestic cats.
label: False

claim: The Mississippi River reverses its flow direction twice daily due to tidal forces from the Gulf of Mexico, with water flowing northward toward Minnesota during high tide and resuming its southward flow during low tide, a phenomenon that has been occurring since the river formed 5 million years ago.
attack: Hydrodynamic dominance: The Mississippi’s average discharge vastly exceeds Gulf tidal forcing except near the mouth, making a twice-daily basin-wide flow reversal physically implausible.
Instrumental records: USGS gauges and current meters along the river do not show periodic northward flow; observations consistently record downstream (southward) flow outside rare extreme events.
Topographic gradient: The river runs downhill from Minnesota to sea level; a routine northward flow would require Gulf water to rise above extensive upstream elevations, which tides cannot achieve.
Limited tidal reach: Tidal influence in the Mississippi is confined to the lower reaches near the delta and does not propagate anywhere near Minnesota, precluding a river-length reversal.
Event-specific reversals only: Documented temporary reversals (e.g., during hurricanes or major storm surges) are exceptional and not semi-diurnal phenomena tied to regular tides.

Geologic timescale inconsistency: The Mississippi’s course and drainage evolved significantly over the last few million years (e.g., glacial reorganizations), so a stable twice-daily reversal “since 5 million years ago” is historically inaccurate.
Infrastructure constraints: Locks and dams on the upper river regulate water levels and flows; a twice-daily reversal would disrupt operations and navigation, which has not been observed.
label: False

claim: The process of photosynthesis in plants releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere while absorbing oxygen from the air, which is the opposite of cellular respiration in animals and explains why forests contribute to increased greenhouse gas concentrations.
attack: Established stoichiometry shows photosynthesis consumes CO2 and produces O2 (6 CO2 + 6 H2O + light → C6H12O6 + 6 O2), directly contradicting the claim’s direction of gas exchange.
Direct gas-exchange measurements on illuminated leaves show net CO2 uptake and O2 release through stomata, refuting the assertion that photosynthesis releases CO2 and absorbs O2.

Ecosystem-scale flux data from eddy-covariance towers consistently record forests as net CO2 sinks over growing seasons, contradicting the claim that forests increase atmospheric greenhouse gases under normal conditions.
Atmospheric records display a seasonal anti-correlation between CO2 and O2 (CO2 falls and O2 rises during the growing season), a fingerprint of terrestrial photosynthesis that opposes the claim.
Remote sensing of solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (a proxy for photosynthetic activity) temporally aligns with declines in atmospheric CO2, inconsistent with the claim’s proposed effect.
label: False

claim: The periodic table of elements is organized by atomic weight from lightest to heaviest, which is why hydrogen appears in the top left corner and oganesson in the bottom right, with each element weighing exactly twice as much as the element immediately preceding it in the sequence.
attack: The periodic table is ordered by atomic number (proton count), not by atomic weight; this was established by Moseley’s work, and the sequence strictly increases by proton number rather than mass.

Atomic weights do not increase monotonically across the table: argon (≈39.95) precedes potassium (≈39.10), cobalt (≈58.93) precedes nickel (≈58.69), and tellurium (≈127.60) precedes iodine (≈126.90), contradicting a weight-based ordering.

The claim that each element weighs exactly twice as much as the previous is immediately falsified numerically: hydrogen (~1.008) followed by helium (~4.002) is not a doubling, and doubling helium (~8) does not match lithium (~6.94); this pattern fails throughout.
Atomic weights are not fixed exact values; they are weighted averages of isotopic abundances that vary by source and are sometimes given as intervals, making an exact doubling relation impossible.

The table’s layout wraps across periods of different lengths; positions do not follow a simple top-left to bottom-right mass gradient. Oganesson’s bottom-right placement follows its atomic number (118) and period structure, not a mass rule.

Chemical periodicity (recurrence of properties) aligns with atomic number, not mass. Historical corrections (e.g., placing Te before I despite heavier mass) show that mass-based ordering fails while atomic-number ordering preserves true periodic trends.
label: False

claim: The human tongue is divided into distinct regions called taste zones, with sweetness detected only at the tip, bitterness exclusively at the back, saltiness along the sides, and sourness detected in two small patches located halfway between the tip and the back, a mapping system that has been confirmed through neurological studies since the 1950s.
attack: Psychophysical testing shows people can detect sweetness, bitterness, saltiness, and sourness across most of the tongue surface, contradicting the claim of mutually exclusive detection zones.

Molecular studies find receptors for sweet, bitter, sour, salty, and umami distributed across multiple papilla types (fungiform, foliate, circumvallate), not confined to the specific regions asserted by the claim.

Electrophysiological recordings from gustatory nerves (e.g., chorda tympani, glossopharyngeal) reveal broadly tuned responses to multiple taste modalities from different tongue locations, refuting exclusive regional mapping.
Clinical observations show that localized nerve blocks or lesions at the tongue tip or back do not selectively abolish just one taste quality, which would be expected if strict zones existed.
